name: Rib cartilage graft rhinoplasty

lead: Rib cartilage rhinoplasty uses cartilage taken from your own rib to build or support the nose when the septum cannot supply enough. People turn to it for major dorsal reconstruction and revision surgery, where a lot of strong structural material is needed to rebuild the bridge or nose shape.
In looksmaxxing discussion it appears as the structural-support option within nose surgery. Evidence comes from retrospective series, including a 58-patient cohort reporting stable results.

paras: Cartilage is harvested from the rib, carved into grafts such as dorsal onlays or columellar struts, and placed in the nose. The rebuilt shape shows after healing.
The procedure adds a second surgical site on the chest, and studies track donor site morbidity, graft warping and revision need. It is performed by surgeons under general anaesthesia.

angle.text: Rib cartilage grafts give substantial structural material, from your own tissue, for major nose rebuilds such as dorsal reconstruction or revision surgery. The cartilage is carved and placed to rebuild the bridge or nose shape, visible after healing. Evidence comes mainly from surgical case series.

lead: Rib (costal) cartilage graft rhinoplasty is a form of nose surgery in which cartilage harvested from the patient's own ribs is carved into grafts to support or build up the nose. It is used when a large amount of structural material is needed, for example in major dorsal reconstruction or revision surgery.[1][2]
In looksmaxxing discussion it appears as the structural-support option within hardmaxxing nose surgery. Published evidence consists of retrospective surgical series.

paras: Wikipedia's rhinoplasty article states that surgeons usually take cartilage from the septum first and use ear or rib cartilage when more is required, as often occurs in revision surgery.[3] A 2015 paper describes a rib graft technique for anchoring an extended columellar strut.[2]

A retrospective cohort study of 58 patients who had osseocartilaginous rib grafts for dorsal augmentation between 2000 and 2009 assessed graft viability, warping, projection, airway function, revisions and donor site morbidity, concluding the technique was stable and predictable for major dorsal reconstruction.[1] A registered study examined allograft cartilage use in cosmetic and reconstructive rhinoplasty (n=50).[4]
